title: Photosynthesis: effect of light intensity
aim: To investigate the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed, by counting the bubbles of oxygen produced with a lamp at different distances.
background: Photosynthesis is an endothermic reaction in which plants use energy transferred from the environment by light to convert carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen: carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen. Aquatic plants such as pondweed (Elodea or Cabomba) release oxygen as bubbles from their cut stems, so the number of bubbles produced per minute can be used to measure the rate of photosynthesis.

The rate of photosynthesis can be limited by temperature, carbon dioxide concentration, light intensity and the amount of chlorophyll. In this practical light intensity is changed by moving a lamp closer to or further from the pondweed. Sodium hydrogencarbonate is added to the water to provide plenty of carbon dioxide, so that carbon dioxide does not limit the rate.

Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the light source: light intensity ∝ 1 ÷ distance². This is the inverse square law (Higher tier). Doubling the distance from the lamp reduces the light intensity to one quarter, not one half.
hypothesis: As the distance between the lamp and the pondweed decreases (so light intensity increases), the rate of photosynthesis will increase, until another factor such as carbon dioxide concentration or temperature becomes limiting.

variables.independent: Light intensity, changed by altering the distance between the lamp and the pondweed (10, 20, 30, 40 and 50 cm).
variables.dependent: Rate of photosynthesis, measured as the number of oxygen bubbles released per minute.
control: Same piece of pondweed (same species, length and number of leaves)
Same concentration and volume of sodium hydrogencarbonate solution (carbon dioxide supply)
Same temperature of the water around the pondweed
Same lamp and bulb (same power and colour of light)
Same time allowed for the pondweed to adjust (5 minutes) and same counting time (1 minute)
Background light kept constant by working in a darkened room

equipment: Pondweed (Elodea or Cabomba), about 10 cm long
Lamp (an LED lamp gives off very little heat)
Beaker of water to act as a heat shield (if a filament lamp is used)
Paper clip (to weigh down the pondweed)
method: In a darkened room, set up a clamp stand and clamp a boiling tube upright next to the end of a metre ruler.
Fill the boiling tube with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution.

Cut a 10 cm piece of pondweed with scissors, making a fresh, slanting cut at the end of the stem. Attach a paper clip to keep it under the solution, and place it in the tube with the cut end at the top.
Place a metre ruler on the bench and position the lamp so that the front of the bulb is 10 cm from the pondweed.
If using a filament lamp, place a beaker of water between the lamp and the tube to absorb heat. Measure the temperature of the solution with a thermometer.
Switch on the lamp and leave the pondweed for 5 minutes so it can adjust to the new light intensity.
Start the stopwatch and count the number of bubbles released from the cut end of the stem in 1 minute.
Repeat the count twice more at the same distance and calculate the mean number of bubbles per minute.
Move the lamp to 20 cm from the pondweed. Check that the temperature of the solution has not changed, leave for 5 minutes, then count bubbles in 1 minute three times.
Repeat for distances of 30, 40 and 50 cm.
Record the results in a table, and plot a graph of mean number of bubbles per minute (y-axis) against distance (x-axis), or against relative light intensity (1 ÷ distance²) for Higher tier.

safety.risk: The bulb gets hot and can cause burns; electricity near water could cause an electric shock.
safety.precaution: Use an LED lamp where possible, do not touch the bulb, keep water and wet hands away from the lamp and plug, and wipe up spills immediately.

safety.risk: Tripping over bags, stools or cables.
safety.precaution: Clear bags and stools away from walkways and tuck cables safely away before the lights are turned off.

safety.risk: Cuts from scissors or broken glass.
safety.precaution: Cut the pondweed on the bench away from your hands, and clamp the boiling tube securely so it cannot fall.
Wash hands after handling the pondweed.

results.notes: Relative light intensity is calculated using the inverse square law, light intensity ∝ 1 ÷ d². Multiplying by 10 000 gives convenient numbers: at 20 cm, 10 000 ÷ 20² = 25. Plot mean bubbles per minute against distance (a curve that falls as distance increases) or against relative light intensity (a curve that rises steeply and then starts to level off).

analysis: As the distance from the lamp increased from 10 cm to 50 cm, the mean number of bubbles per minute decreased from 50 to 6. This shows that as light intensity decreases, the rate of photosynthesis decreases.
Light provides the energy for photosynthesis. At low light intensities, light is the limiting factor, so increasing the light intensity increases the rate of photosynthesis.

When the results are plotted against relative light intensity, the rate rises steeply at low intensities (from 6 to 17 bubbles per minute between intensities of 4 and 11.1) but much less steeply at high intensities (from 31 to 50 bubbles per minute between 25 and 100). The curve begins to level off because another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration, temperature or the amount of chlorophyll, has become limiting.
Moving the lamp from 10 cm to 20 cm reduces the light intensity to a quarter (inverse square law), which is why the rate changes so much at short distances.
The bubbles may contain some gases other than oxygen, and bubble size varies, so bubble counts are an estimate of the rate of oxygen production rather than an exact measurement.

errors.error: Bubbles are not all the same size, so counting bubbles does not measure the volume of oxygen accurately; bubbles may also be released too quickly to count at short distances.
errors.improvement: Collect the gas in an upturned measuring cylinder or a gas syringe (photosynthometer) and measure the volume produced in a set time.

errors.error: Heat from a filament lamp can raise the temperature of the water, so temperature changes as well as light intensity.
errors.improvement: Use an LED lamp, or place a beaker of water as a heat shield between the lamp and the tube, and check the temperature with a thermometer at each distance.

errors.error: Light from windows or other groups' lamps changes the light reaching the pondweed.
errors.improvement: Carry out the investigation in a darkened room, with the lamp as the only light source.

errors.error: Carbon dioxide in the solution is used up over time, so it may become limiting during the experiment.
errors.improvement: Use fresh sodium hydrogencarbonate solution of the same concentration and keep the total time of the experiment short.

examTips: Higher tier: light intensity ∝ 1 ÷ d². If the distance doubles, the light intensity becomes one quarter. If the distance halves, the intensity becomes four times greater.
Explain why temperature must be controlled (it also affects the rate of photosynthesis) and how: use an LED lamp or a heat shield, and check with a thermometer.
When the graph levels off, say that light intensity is no longer the limiting factor and name another factor that is now limiting (carbon dioxide concentration or temperature).
Measuring the volume of gas in a gas syringe or measuring cylinder is more accurate than counting bubbles, because bubbles differ in size.
Remember the gas produced is oxygen, a product of photosynthesis, and sodium hydrogencarbonate supplies carbon dioxide.

questions.question: Which gas is mainly found in the bubbles released by the pondweed in bright light?
options: Carbon dioxide
Nitrogen
Oxygen
Water vapour
markScheme: 1 mark: oxygen
questions.explanation: Oxygen is a product of photosynthesis. Carbon dioxide is used up in photosynthesis, so it is not released in bright light. The bubbles may contain small amounts of other gases, but they are mostly oxygen.

questions.question: Why is sodium hydrogencarbonate added to the water around the pondweed?
options: To provide carbon dioxide so that it does not limit the rate of photosynthesis
To keep the pH of the water at its optimum
To provide glucose for the pondweed
To absorb heat from the lamp
markScheme: 1 mark: it releases (provides) carbon dioxide, so carbon dioxide is not a limiting factor
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is a reactant in photosynthesis. Providing plenty of it means the rate depends on light intensity, the variable being tested. Plants make their own glucose, and heat is absorbed by a heat shield, not by the solution.

questions.question:
In this investigation, the pondweed is left for 5 minutes after the lamp is moved, before the bubbles are counted.
Give the reason for this.
acceptedAnswers: to adjust to new light intensity
markScheme: 1 mark: to allow the pondweed to adjust to the new light intensity (so the rate of photosynthesis becomes steady)
questions.explanation: The rate does not change instantly when light intensity changes. Waiting allows the rate to settle so the count reflects the new light intensity.

The student used a filament lamp.
Why should a beaker of water be placed between the lamp and the pondweed?

options: To reduce the light intensity reaching the pondweed
To provide extra water for photosynthesis
To absorb heat so the temperature of the pondweed stays constant
To focus the light onto the pondweed
markScheme: 1 mark: to absorb heat from the lamp (so temperature does not change and is controlled)
questions.explanation: Filament lamps give out a lot of heat, especially when close. Temperature also affects the rate of photosynthesis, so it must be kept constant. Using an LED lamp is another way to avoid this problem.

questions.question:
A student counted the number of bubbles released by pondweed with the lamp 20 cm away.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the mean number of bubbles per minute.
questions.explanation: Add the three counts (93) and divide by 3 to give a mean of 31 bubbles per minute.

questions.question:
The lamp is 20 cm from the pondweed.
Calculate the relative light intensity.
Use the equation:
relative light intensity = 1 ÷ d²
where d is the distance from the lamp in cm.
questions.explanation: Square the distance first (20² = 400), then divide 1 by it: 0.0025. Dividing 1 by 20 (giving 0.05) forgets to square the distance.

questions.question:
A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 30 cm away from the pondweed.
Light intensity is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the lamp.
Calculate how many times lower the light intensity becomes.
markScheme: 1 mark: distance increases by a factor of 3
1 mark: intensity decreases by a factor of 3² = 9
questions.explanation: Light intensity ∝ 1 ÷ d². Tripling the distance divides the intensity by 3² = 9. A common error is to think it falls by a factor of 3.

questions.question:
A student improved the investigation by collecting the oxygen in a gas syringe.
Figure 1 shows the gas syringe after 4 minutes. The syringe was empty at the start.
Calculate the rate of oxygen production in cm³ per minute.

questions.explanation: The plunger is 2 small divisions past 2 cm³ and each small division is 0.2 cm³, so 2.4 cm³ of oxygen was collected. Rate = volume of gas ÷ time = 2.4 ÷ 4 = 0.6 cm³ per minute.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows bubbles of gas being released by a piece of pondweed.
Counting bubbles is not a very accurate way to measure the rate of photosynthesis.
Give one reason why.
Suggest a better method.

acceptedAnswers: collect gas in a gas syringe
markScheme: 1 mark: bubbles are different sizes (or are released too quickly to count accurately)
1 mark: collect the gas and measure its volume, for example with a gas syringe or upturned measuring cylinder
questions.explanation: Two bubbles might contain very different volumes of oxygen. Measuring total volume avoids this problem and gives more accurate results.

markScheme: 1 mark: light intensity is no longer the limiting factor
1 mark: another factor, such as carbon dioxide concentration, temperature or amount of chlorophyll, is now limiting the rate
questions.explanation: Increasing a factor only increases the rate while that factor is limiting. Once something else is in short supply, extra light makes little difference.

questions.question: What is the dependent variable in an investigation into the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed?
options: The distance of the lamp from the pondweed
The temperature of the water
The concentration of sodium hydrogencarbonate
The number of bubbles produced per minute
markScheme: 1 mark: number of bubbles per minute (rate of oxygen production)
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is what is measured: bubbles per minute. Distance is the independent variable, while temperature and sodium hydrogencarbonate concentration are control variables.

questions.question: Explain why this investigation should be carried out in a darkened room.
markScheme: 1 mark: so that the only light reaching the pondweed is from the lamp
1 mark: so light intensity depends only on the distance from the lamp (other light would change the light intensity)
questions.explanation: Daylight or other lamps add extra light that changes during the lesson, so the distance from the lamp would no longer control the light intensity.

questions.question:
A lamp is moved from 40 cm to 20 cm from some pondweed.
What happens to the light intensity at the pondweed?
options: It doubles
It becomes four times greater
It halves
It becomes one quarter
markScheme: 1 mark: it becomes four times greater
questions.explanation: Light intensity ∝ 1 ÷ d². Halving the distance multiplies the intensity by 2² = 4. Students who think the relationship is simply inverse would wrongly say it doubles.

questions.question: Describe a method to investigate how light intensity affects the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed.
markScheme: Indicative content: place pondweed in a boiling tube of sodium hydrogencarbonate solution (to provide carbon dioxide), clamped; place a lamp a measured distance away using a metre ruler (for example 10 cm); darkened room; use LED lamp or heat shield and check temperature with thermometer; leave for 5 minutes to adjust; count bubbles released in 1 minute (or collect gas in a gas syringe and measure volume); repeat count three times and calculate mean; move lamp to 20, 30, 40, 50 cm and repeat; control: same pondweed, same temperature, same carbon dioxide concentration, same lamp; plot rate against distance or against 1 ÷ d²

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, logically ordered method that would produce valid results, describing how light intensity is varied, how the rate is measured, and how at least two variables (including temperature) are controlled.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a method with most key steps, but missing some detail of control variables, repeats or measurement.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements such as moving a lamp and counting bubbles, with little detail.
0 marks: no relevant content.
questions.explanation: Strong answers describe the full sequence: set-up, changing distance, waiting, measuring, repeating and controlling temperature and carbon dioxide.

questions.question:
Table 1 shows the results of an investigation into the effect of light intensity on the rate of photosynthesis in pondweed.
Explain these results.
Refer to light intensity and photosynthesis in your answer.

headers: Mean number of bubbles per minute

markScheme: Indicative content: as distance increases, light intensity decreases; light intensity ∝ 1 ÷ d², so doubling distance from 10 to 20 cm reduces light intensity to a quarter; light provides the energy for photosynthesis (absorbed by chlorophyll); less light means less energy transferred, so less photosynthesis and less oxygen released; light is the limiting factor at greater distances; the rate did not fall to a quarter between 10 and 20 cm because at 10 cm another factor (such as carbon dioxide or temperature) was partly limiting
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): links increasing distance to decreasing light intensity (with the inverse square law) and explains reduced photosynthesis in terms of light energy and limiting factors.
